stories.headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang days after his exit, with Trump claiming credit
stories.text:
Nvidia, the chipmaker at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday 23 November. The BBC reports that the company said senior US government officials backed the decision (927577a8194d). Huang had resigned days earlier amid allegations, reported by the Guardian, of three affairs, one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset and two with employees (df0b7b27e673).

The reversal was abrupt. The Guardian's Nils Pratley, writing as opinion, notes that the board's new chair, Harvey Jones, had said only six days earlier that the board did not intend to bring Huang back, and that the board had not finished its investigation (a99aec6f3c0e). Singapore's prime minister, Lawrence Wong, said Singapore had investigated the woman named in the reports, Alice Huang, but released her because there was no basis for prosecution (c8b

stories.headline: A violent swing in AI shares: Friday's global sell-off, Monday's rebound, and fears that remain
stories.text:
Market data show the S&P 500, the index of 500 large US companies, closed at 7,237.17 on 23 November, up 4.73% on the day, yet still down 2.42% over five days and 5.07% over a month, and about 7% below its 52-week high of 7,818.93. The BBC reports that Nvidia's value rose by almost $1tn and the tech-heavy Nasdaq rose 6.5% (812d2a85a0ba). The Guardian reports Nvidia's rise at about a third (52127ca3d657).

The jump followed a bad stretch. The Guardian says global markets tumbled on Friday 20 November and the Nasdaq closed 5% below its 1 January level, with investors getting 'cold feet' about AI companies (c6e842f1b8c5). Supplied data show Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 5.06% on 20 November and was down 12.67% over a month. Note: the Nasdaq 100 figure in the data (-2.21%, 19 November) is stale and pre-dates the rebound. stories.headline: Fed's Williams says higher interest rates likely 'over time' to tackle inflation
stories.text:
John Williams, an influential Federal Reserve official, indicated that higher interest rates are likely 'over time' to address inflation, while expressing confidence that inflation will move closer to the Fed's 2% target in 2027 (CNBC, 8642b27e9894). Only the headline and summary are supplied, so we do not have his full remarks or any timing.

Supplied macro data show US consumer price inflation at 4.08% year on year (October data point), the Fed funds rate at 3.88%, unemployment at 4.1%, and real GDP growth of 2.07% year on year. The US 10-year Treasury yield was 4.92% on 23 November, below its 52-week high of 5.31%. The gap between 10-year and 2-year yields was 0.28 percentage points. The Conference Board's consumer confidence index rose to 103.3, with CNBC linking the improvement to Democrats' midterm victories while noting inflation worries persist (a94fd2384b2f). stories.headline: Trump reportedly readies new tariffs on China, EU, Japan and South Korea
stories.text: The Financial Times reports, in a headline and summary only, that President Trump is preparing a raft of new tariffs, with China, the EU, Japan and South Korea expected to be hit as he 'doubles down' on his trade strategy (1ebf874f7500). No rates, dates or products are supplied, and this is a single source. Unconfirmed for now: details matter, and until the White House publishes them this remains a one-outlet report.

stories.headline: EU edges towards a 'Made in Europe' deal covering UK cars
stories.text:
The Financial Times reports the EU is edging towards including UK-built cars in its 'Made in Europe' subsidy scheme, which would be a diplomatic win for Prime Minister Andy Burnham (90f74592807f). The Guardian reports the Irish EU presidency has proposed giving the UK 'partner' status on car assembly, and that the UK would not have to apply the EU's tariffs on Chinese car imports (f2bacd55c1a0). Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told a parliamentary committee there had been 'a transformation in the EU view'.

The Guardian's podcast item says options for how Britain could rejoin the EU will not be outlined until December (caf9878dcf91). Separately, the Guardian reports that Agratas's £5.2bn Bridgwater battery gigafactory, meant to supply Jaguar Land Rover, has lost its second building contractor in five months (aef8ec94c7f5). These are proposals, not agreements. Diplomatic progress on car-ind

stories.headline: EU warns France and Belgium on public finances as French recession risk is debated
stories.text: The Financial Times reports the European Commission has warned France and Belgium to put their public finances on a 'sustainable path', and that Germany could face additional monitoring next year owing to excessive public spending (dfa1b1eb65d4). CNBC reports Bank of France Governor Emmanuel Moulin still expects growth, citing resilience in defence, aerospace and electricity, in a piece about France's recession risk (8aad6a2decd0). The BBC reports strikes cancelling flights in Belgium as the prime minister struggles to agree a budget to cut costs (963d3ef7d709). Brussels is pressing governments to cut deficits just as growth is uncertain.

stories.headline: Compass Group plans to move its main listing from London to New York
stories.text: Compass Group, the world's largest catering group, confirmed it plans to move its primary stock-market listing to the US, saying it has become 'a predominantly North American business' and wants access to 'the world's largest and deepest pool of capital'. It has begun consulting shareholders, two-fifths of whom are US-based (7343f381c0f0). The Guardian's Nils Pratley (opinion) says the switch is planned for 2028, that Compass is the 18th largest FTSE 100 company, and calls the logic 'flimsy' while criticising ministers for not doing more to stop such departures (5848cd8f3262). Another blue-chip is leaving London; the company says it is about its US footprint.

stories.headline: UK disability benefit review points to 'fundamental overhaul' of Pip assessments
stories.text: Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms is to recommend major reform of the personal independence payment (Pip), saying assessments need a 'fundamental overhaul' (BBC, 915494bd598f). The review was commissioned last year after the government was forced to water down planned benefit cuts (a3d851196d64). The Financial Times headline says Prime Minister Burnham has been warned the review risks increasing a £40bn bill, and that the government will try to reconcile it with a separate report last week by Alan Milburn (0a36b696aa6c). Detailed figures are not in the supplied text. Reform is coming, but its fiscal effect is still unclear.

stories.headline: Oil prices well below recent highs, but diesel and jet fuel stay tight
stories.text: The FT says the energy market is both tight and loose: inflationary pressure remains in diesel and jet fuel prices despite a glut of gasoline (9695a7135df7). It also reports that Iraq's government is to take control of Kurdish-held oilfields (b34835691a3f). Latest supplied (but stale, 17 November) oil prices: WTI $89.53 and Brent $92.94, down about 18.6% and 21.8% over a month, though Brent's 52-week high was $138.21. Crude has fallen sharply but fuel inflation has not gone away.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia chief executive after Trump intervention; shares jump, then give back ground
stories.text:
Nvidia's board reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday 23 November. He had been ousted after allegations of three affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset (the Guardian, df0b7b27e673). The BBC reported that Nvidia's market value rose by almost $1tn on the news and that the tech-heavy Nasdaq rose 6.5% (812d2a85a0ba). The Guardian put the share-price gain at about a third (52127ca3d657 is an opinion piece; db8fd0076e40 is the news report). The two outlets give different framings of the size of the move, so treat the exact figure with caution.

President Trump said he had 'convinced' Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang and faced backlash for it (BBC, 9c30b79cef44). The Financial Times headline says Trump helped 'orchestrate' the return (609750e23086). The Guardian reported that Trump made up to $15m on his own Nvidia holdings after the jump (d

stories.headline: AI-linked shares struggle to hold gains: Anthropic slips below IPO price, Micron and HPE fall
stories.text:
Anthropic's shares closed below their $83 IPO price for the first time, less than a week after listing on the Nasdaq (MarketWatch, 48cdb2269afe; FT headline, 1a3f0c993b77, which says investor relief over Huang's reinstatement had subsided). Micron fell after a BNP Paribas analyst warned that the risk of 'an oversupply scenario' in memory chips is mounting and could threaten its pricing power (af91f039806c). Hewlett Packard Enterprise raised its forecast on Monday on strong AI demand and posted what MarketWatch calls its strongest growth ever, yet its stock fell (e9db46d704a6).

Commentary adds to the caution. The BBC's Faisal Islam argues that fears about the AI boom existed before Huang's exit and his return 'won't fix' them (f5b8a2db69f0, opinion). A MarketWatch column argues equities remain 'hardly cheap' despite declines over recent weeks (8ae1fd21b525, opinion). The Economist's head

stories.headline: Fed's Williams says higher rates likely 'over time' as US inflation stays above 4%
stories.text:
CNBC reported that New York Fed president John Williams indicated higher interest rates are likely 'over time' to address inflation, and expressed confidence that inflation will get closer to the Fed's 2% target in 2027 (8642b27e9894). This is a single-outlet report and the evidence includes only the headline and summary, not his full remarks.

Latest supplied macro data show US consumer price inflation at 4.08% year on year, the Fed funds rate at 3.88%, unemployment at 4.1% and the 10-year Treasury yield at 4.92% (23 November close). The Fed also published minutes of its Board's discount rate meetings on 19 and 28 October (a22a480c189f); the supplied item carries no detail on the contents.

stories.headline: Trump reported to be readying fresh tariffs on China, the EU, Japan and South Korea
stories.text:
The Financial Times reported, in a headline and summary only, that Trump is readying a raft of new tariffs on major economies. China, the EU, Japan and South Korea are expected to be hit as the president 'doubles down on trade strategy' (1ebf874f7500). No rates, start dates or product lists appear in the evidence, and no other supplied outlet corroborates this. Treat it as a single-source report of an expected measure, not a confirmed policy.

The Economist has a piece asking whether America's supply chains are more vulnerable than China's (099bb4d72302; headline only), which shows the debate about trade dependence is live. A reported but unconfirmed tariff round would push on the inflation problem the Fed is already worried about.

stories.headline: Houthi strike on Riyadh, Iraqi move on Kurdish oilfields and a split fuel market keep energy risk alive
stories.text:
The FT reported that a Houthi attack on the PIF Tower in Riyadh, headquarters of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, injured 11. It came as the kingdom unveiled its first budget since conflict with the Iran-backed rebels restarted (5b235bc86e40; headline and summary only). The FT also reported that Iraq's government will take control of Kurdish-held oilfields as the prime minister works to assert power over the semi-autonomous Kurdish region and Iran-backed Shia militias (b34835691a3f).

An FT analysis says the energy market is 'both tight and loose': inflationary pressure remains in diesel and jet fuel despite a glut of gasoline (9695a7135df7).

The most recent supplied oil prices are stale (17 November): Brent $92.94, down 21.78% over a month and far below its 52-week high of $138.21; WTI $89.53. They do not reflect these events. Oil is well below its peak but fuel-product tightness

stories.headline: EU presses France and Belgium on public finances as France's recession risk is debated
stories.text:
The European Commission warned France and Belgium to put their public finances on a 'sustainable path' and warned Germany it could face additional monitoring next year owing to excessive public spending (FT, dfa1b1eb65d4; headline and summary only).

CNBC reported that Bank of France Governor Emmanuel Moulin still expects growth, pointing to resilience in defence, aerospace and electricity, in a piece on why France is at risk of recession (8aad6a2decd0). The supplied summary gives no growth numbers. Tight budgets and weak growth is a difficult combination for Europe's big economies.

stories.headline: Compass Group plans to move its main listing from London to New York
stories.text: Compass Group, the world's largest catering group, confirmed plans to move its primary stock-market listing to the US, saying it had become 'a predominantly North American business' and that New York offers 'the world's largest and deepest pool of capital' (Guardian, 7343f381c0f0). It has begun consulting shareholders, about two-fifths of whom are in the US. Guardian columnist Nils Pratley says the switch is planned for 2028, that Compass is the 18th largest FTSE 100 company and that its logic is 'flimsy' (5848cd8f3262; opinion). London's listing problem continues, with a well-known FTSE 100 name heading to New York.

stories.headline: Nvidia's 30% surge on Jensen Huang's return fades as politics and export-control questions move in
stories.text:
Technology shares led a market retreat on Tuesday 24 November. The previous day, Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive, days after he was forced to resign, had pushed Nvidia shares up by more than 30% and added more than $900bn to its market value (The Guardian). By Tuesday's close the stock had lost almost 6% (The Guardian). The BBC puts the fall at 7%. The gap is probably a matter of timing or measurement, and we do not know which. Both outlets agree on the direction.

The return has become a political issue. Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer accused Huang of shipping "extremely advanced chips to China" and violating US export control laws. Schumer said this "amounts to the equivalent of selling rocket engines to the Soviets during the space race". These are his accusations, not findings by any court or agency. stories.headline: Anthropic closes below its $83 IPO price within a week as AI-hardware signals turn mixed
stories.text:
Shares in Anthropic traded below their IPO price of $83 for the first time, less than a week after their Nasdaq debut (MarketWatch). The FT reports it closed below the offer price on Tuesday as the tech rally faded.

Earnings from the AI supply chain gave mixed signals. Dell's stock rose as AI demand helped sales more than double. Dell says its backlog is "rigorously vetted for customer quality and access to capital, land and power" (MarketWatch). HPE posted its strongest growth ever and raised its forecast, yet its stock is sinking. Micron fell after a BNP Paribas analyst warned that the risk of an "oversupply scenario is mounting" in memory chips, which could threaten its pricing power. That is one analyst's opinion.

stories.headline: US reported to be preparing a new round of tariffs on major trading partners, including China and the EU
stories.text:
The BBC reports that the US is preparing to unveil a plan for new tariffs, which are taxes on imports, on global trading partners. The new levies would hit many of America's biggest partners, including China and the EU. An FT newsletter likewise says Trump "readies a raft of new tariffs". No rates, products or start dates appear in our evidence, so the scale is unknown.

Separately, the FT reports that China has issued a list of demands to Brussels over EU trade talks. It also reports that the EU plans a €50bn fund to take stakes in AI and quantum computing companies to narrow the gap with the US and China. We have only the headlines, with no detail on the Chinese demands or the fund's design. A new US tariff round is reportedly coming. The details, which will determine the economic effect, are not yet public.

stories.headline: Houthi strike on Riyadh's PIF Tower injures 11 as Saudi Arabia unveils its budget
stories.text:
The FT reports that a Houthi attack on the Riyadh headquarters of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, the PIF, injured 11 people. It came as the kingdom unveiled its first budget since the conflict with the Iran-backed rebels restarted. Our evidence includes only the FT headline and standfirst. It is a single source, and we have no detail on damage or any official response.

Oil prices are very sensitive to the Gulf region. On 24 November WTI closed at $82.24 (+1.01% on the day) and Brent at $91.80 (+0.66%). Over a month Brent is down 28.35% and WTI down 21.86%. Both remain well below their 52-week highs of $138.21 and $114.58. A single-source report of an attack on a Saudi financial target adds a risk to the oil outlook. The month's fall in crude shows how much the price can move either way.

stories.headline: The FT expects more ECB tightening as eurozone capitals try to settle the bank's top job
stories.text:
The FT's Monetary Policy Radar team publishes a November scenario titled "Further tightening to come from the ECB to prevent inflation persistence". We have only the headline. It is a forecast by one outlet, not an ECB statement. The ECB has not announced any move in our evidence.

Separately, the FT reports that eurozone capitals are seeking a "consolation prize" for Dutch contender Knot so that there is no ECB vote. Leaders are preparing to endorse his Spanish rival to head the central bank. This is a single-source report on a decision that has not been made.

The ECB also announced that it and Sveriges Riksbank concluded an agreement for Sweden to join T2, the euro area's payment system for large transfers (primary source). It is a technical item with no direct bearing on interest rates. The FT forecasts more ECB tightening, and the political process for choosing the next ECB head is

stories.headline: Poundland collapses into administration and Ofgem raises the energy price cap, a double blow to UK households
stories.text:
Poundland has called in administrators from AlixPartners, putting jobs at risk before Christmas. The Guardian says 12,000 jobs are at risk and the BBC says 11,000. The chain has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland. The Guardian reports that its US owner, Gordon Brothers, rejected at least two last-ditch bids. The BBC says the owners failed to find a buyer. These accounts differ, and we cannot tell which is right. The chain is expected to be broken up, with significant job losses and store closures (The Guardian).

The BBC also reports that domestic gas prices will rise significantly in January under regulator Ofgem's new price cap, which limits the unit price suppliers can charge on standard tariffs. It says millions of households will receive a £100 energy payment from January. We have no cap figure or payment details in our evidence. Both the retail failure and the energy cap hit the same

stories.headline: Nationwide offers 99% mortgages to first-time buyers, drawing warnings about negative equity
stories.text:
Nationwide unveiled a mortgage on Wednesday that lets first-time buyers buy a home with a 1% deposit. Borrowers could potentially borrow up to six times their income (The Guardian, FT headline).

The Guardian reports that brokers have warned that even a small fall in house prices could leave borrowers in negative equity, which means owing more than the home is worth. Easier access to a mortgage helps buyers but raises the cost of a house-price fall, and the brokers' warnings point to that trade-off.
